Criminal Appeal No. 944 of 1991 (Dhaka) 
Criminal Appeal No. 140 of 1985 (Bakerganj)
lawyer:
Kitab Ali Talukder vs. State 28 DLR 128; State vs. Badsha Mollah 41 DLR 11 
Syed Ziaul Karim, Advocate—For the Appellant AKM Shamsul Karim, Assistant Attorney-General—For the State
parties:
Munsurul Hossain  ----- Appellant
Vs.
State ----- opposite Party
full_judgment:
6. Upon consideration of the evidence on record the learned Sessions Judge convicted the appellant in his absence under section 302 of the Penal Code and sentenced him to imprisonment for life by judgment and order, dated 24-12-84 and the learned Sessions Judge, however, acquitted other accused persons giving them benefit of doubt. 

 Section 512 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides for recording of evidence against a person accused of an offence in his absence. It reads as follows : 

 512(1) "If it is proved that an accused person has absconded, and that there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, the court competent to try such person for the offence complained of may, in his absence, examine the witnesses (if any) produced on behalf of the prosecution and record their depositions. Any such deposition may be given in evidence against him on the inquiry into or trial for the offence with which he is charged, if the deponent is dead or incapable of giving evidence or his attendance cannot be procured without an amount of delay, expense or inconvenience which under the circumstances of the case would be unreasonable." 

 11. In the instant case the appellant absconded from the very beginning and trial was held in his absence. From the order sheet it appears that proclamation and attachment was served against him and there has been compliance of the provision of section 339B of the Code of Criminal Procedure by notifying in the Gazette but he remained absconding till judgment was passed and he was also charged under section 302 and no lawyer was appointed to represent him as per above provisions of law and, as such, the above cited decision is quite applicable in the present case. We may also refer here to another decision of this court reported in 28 DLR 128 in the case of Kitab Ali Talukder vs. State. In that case the complainant lodged a first information report on 3-8-72 alleging commission of certain offences falling under section 380 against Kitab Ali absconding. Accordingly, he was tried in his absence. The tribunal on consideration of the evidence of 9 witnesses for the prosecution held him guilty and convicted and sentenced him to certain terms of imprisonment and payment of fine. 

 "Under the provisions of section 512 (I), Criminal Procedure Code, any evidence recorded against an accused in his absence may be used, when he is brought to trial, in three circumstance; if the witness is dead, or if he is incapable of giving evidence; or if his attendance cannot be procured without unreasonable delay or expense. It is therefore clear that evidence recorded in absence of an accused may be used for a limited purpose. To record evidence even for this limited purpose two conditions precedent are to be fulfilled. It is to be proved that "the accused has absconded" and that" there is no immediate prospect of arresting him." 

 16. The learned Advocate of the appellant, in reply, seriously objected to such submission of the State lawyer, by pointing out that admittedly the appellant was tried in absentia and there is nothing on record to show that the property of the accused were attached although writ of proclamation and attachment were issued and notification in Gazette was made in compliance with the provision of section 339B of the Code, and further submitted that no step was taken to arrest the accused and the trial was concluded in his absence on 13-12-84 and the judgment was delivered on 24-12-84 and thereafter the local police apprehended the accused Babul on 25-9-85 and it appears from record that the accused surrendered before the court on 28-9-85 praying for the certified copy of the judgment free of cost and since then he has been in custody and it will be plainly an act of sheer injustice to make him face a fresh trial after a long lapse of time, only to cross-examine the witnesses including Investigating Officer and the doctor although the other accused persons had already been acquitted by the learned court below giving them benefit of doubt on the same evidence on record and without Investigating Officer and the Doctor being cross-examined and, as such, we do not, therefore, think that this is a fit case of retrial. 

 17. Turning to the merit of the case, Mr. Syed Ziaul Karim, the learned Advocate for the appellant, has submitted that the prosecution witnesses are interested and related and there are inconsistencies in their depositions in all material particulars. No independent and material charge-sheet witnesses were examined to prove the prosecution case. There is no circumstantial evidence against the appellant. He has next submitted that there has been an unusual delay in lodging the First Information Report which has made the prosecution case shaky and doubtful and, as such, the learned Sessions Judge seriously erred in law in passing the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence merely on surmises and conjectures and upon the so-called circumstantial evidence that is, the abscondance of the appellant. Hence the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence should be set aside and the appellant be acquitted of the charge levelled against him. 

 18. Mr. Shamsul Karim, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, on the other hand, submits that, the learned Sessions Judge having considered the oral evidence on record rightly passed the impugned judgement and order of conviction and sentence against the appellant in his absence and there is no delay in lodging the First Information Report and the delay has been properly explained and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence should be upheld and the appeal should be dismissed. 

 19. Now, in order to appreciate the submissions of the learned Advocate for the parties, let us go into the evidence. 

 39. PW 7 Amir Hossain is also said to be a neighbour. He too cannot be relied on. He did not see the alleged assault on Seraj but stated that on hearing cries he went towards the house of Nurul Hoque PW 2 and saw accused Babul and Nurul Hoque running away. In cross-examination he denied that he did not state to Daroga that on Saturday the day of occurrence he was not at his house and gave hearsay evidence. He further stated that above 300/400 persons assembled on that day of occurrence and admitted that the Chairman and Member were not present although it transpired from the deposition of other witnesses that the Chairman and Member were informed about the occurrence but they were not examined and none of the witnesses said about assembly of 300/400 persons on that day and it was not at all the First Information Report case, and he also did not state that about Seraj being senseless and due to assault he was bleeding as disclosed by PWs 1, 3 and 4 who are all relations. 

 42. PW 11 Amir Hossain stated that Mahinur, wife of Seraj, was kept in his house whereas PW 1 stated that Mahinur was kept in the house of Member Serajuddin and PW 8 said Serajuddin and they contradicted each other. From the scrutiny of the aforesaid evidence on record it transpires to us that PWs. 1 to 5 and 10 are close relations and they are not only interested but they made contradictory statements which leave a room for doubt. PWs. 6, 7 and 8 also made contradictory statements and have not supported the PW 1 in material particulars as noticed above and PW I herself made embellishment of the prosecution case made in the First Information Report. It further transpires that doctor who held the post-mortem examination of the deceased has not been examined. 

 44. Further, it appears that the doctor who held the post mortem examination of the deceased, the Investigating Officer and other material witnesses as mentioned above have been withheld and their non-examination casts a serious doubt in the prosecution case. Local Chairman, Member, charge-sheet witness Khalilur Rahman and deceased's wife Mahinur were the material witnesses but they were withheld and if they were examined they would not have supported the prosecution case under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. 

 45. The PWs 1-5 and 10 being relations are highly interested and the PWs 6-8 are said to be independent being neighbours but their evidence also suffers from material infirmities being contradictory and uncorroborative with those of PWs.1-5 and, as such, all the prosecution witnesses are not competent, truthful and reliable and the circumstances of the complicity of the appellant to cause the death of victim Seraj has not been established beyond reasonable doubt. The learned Sessions Judge appears to have convicted and sentenced the appellant only on the ground of his absconsion but mere absconsion cannot alwayes be a circumstances to lead to an inference of guilt of the accused. In this connection reference may be made to the case of State vs. Badsha Mollah reported in 41 DLR 11, wherein their Lordships after reviewing number of decisions of our High Court and the Appellate Division as well as cases of Indian Supreme Court held as under: 

 46. Here in this case the alleged offence against the appellant has not been proved beyond reasonable doubt. From the above decision and from the evidence on record and the circumstances arising therefrom, we are of the view that the appellant is entitled to be acquitted. 

 48. We have given our anxious consideration to the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record and we are of the view that the prosecution has utterly failed to prove the charge against the accused appellant either by reliable and independent witnesses or by sufficient circumstantial evidence beyond all reasonable doubt and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence is liable to be set aside and hence it is set aside
